I've sold over a hundred AI automation systems and I've priced plenty of them wrong. 

In this video I walk through one real build I sold, every number in it, and show you how to turn a client's own numbers into a price you can actually defend. 

I also cover why hourly billing works against you, how to structure milestones so you get paid every 30 days, and who should be paying for API costs.

comments.text: The “hours saved vs bottom-line impact” distinction is especially important for AI automation pricing. In finance, I’d want every proposal to separate build cost, recurring run cost, exception-handling cost, and the actual value driver being improved. That makes the discussion much easier to defend internally than a generic hourly estimate.
comments.author: @Ani-Bjorkstrom

comments.text: Great stuff. Most of the time, I present clients with a few different packages, each with its own set of features. And as you mentioned, they usually end up choosing the middle option.
comments.author: @EldonConceicao

comments.text: The middle-option pull is real, and you can design for it on purpose. I make the top package a bit more than most people need so the middle feels like the sensible choice, and I put the one feature everyone actually wants in the middle tier and up. The anchor does the selling. The trick is making the middle genuinely the best fit, not a trap.
comments.author: @magneticfounders

comments.text: The pricing mistake I made longest was quoting off how hard the build was for me. Clients never feel my hours, they feel the problem that stops happening. The same automation felt cheap when I called it "a workflow" and worth a retainer when I framed it as "you never touch this task again." Nothing changed but the outcome I put the price next to.

comments.text: I've been on the other side of this. A freelance dev quoted me $5,000 to $10,000 for a system I ended up building myself in about 20 hours with Claude Code. That gap between what these systems cost to build and what they're worth to a business is exactly why pricing feels so unsettled right now.
comments.author: @NateNeedham

comments.text: That gap is the whole game now, and it won't settle because the two numbers measure different things. Build cost keeps falling. Business value stays where it always was, tied to the problem being gone. I stopped pricing on hours the day I realized a client will happily pay for an outcome they'd never pay for as a timesheet. Price the result, not the effort.
comments.author: @magneticfounders

comments.text: AI automation is often priced by how many human hours it replaces. But that leaves out the harder question: who carries the risk when the automation makes a costly mistake? The true price should include not only value created, but accountability, oversight, maintenance, and the consequences of failure.
